sections.body_md:
A polyhedron is the set of points that satisfy a finite list of linear inequalities. It may also be written with linear equalities. Each inequality is a half-space, and a half-space contains the segment between any two of its points. An intersection of convex sets is convex, so every polyhedron is convex. The union of two polyhedra need not be.

An extreme point is a point of the set that cannot be written as a strict convex combination of two other points of the set. In the plane, the extreme points of a polygon are the corners. A point in the middle of an edge is the midpoint of a short segment that stays inside the set, so it is not extreme. A vertex, in the sense used here, is a point where enough inequalities are tight, with independent normals, that the point is the unique solution of those equalities, and the remaining inequalities hold.

For a polyhedron written as \(Ax = b\), \(x \ge 0\), with independent rows, these three descriptions name the same points: extreme points, vertices, and basic feasible solutions. A basic feasible solution picks an invertible set of columns, sets the other variables to zero, and keeps \(B^{-1} b \ge 0\).

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
A point \(x\) is not extreme when \(x = (1 - t) y + t z\) for some \(y \ne z\) in the set and some \(t\) strictly between 0 and 1. In a basic feasible solution the basis satisfies
\[
x_B = B^{-1} b \ge 0, \qquad x_N = 0.
\]
A convex weight along a segment from the origin to \((p, 0)\) that lands at \((s, 0)\) is the ratio \(s/p\). The same arithmetic, in higher dimension, is what says an edge point is a combination of the endpoints of that edge.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
The yard is the triangle with vertices \((2, 7)\), \((2, 11)\), and \((10, 7)\), cut out by \(x \ge 2\), \(y \ge 7\), and \(x + 2y \le 24\). Minimize \(x + 9y\). The vertex values are \(2 + 63 = 65\), \(2 + 99 = 101\), and \(10 + 63 = 73\).

The yard value is 65, at \((2, 7)\) only. The point halfway along an edge, for example the midpoint of \((2, 7)\) and \((10, 7)\), is feasible and is not extreme. A linear cost cannot prefer that midpoint to both endpoints.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Calling every boundary point extreme is the usual overcount. Edges are full of boundary points, and only the corners are extreme. A second miss is to expect a polyhedron to be bounded. A half-space is already a polyhedron, and it has no extreme point at all when it is a single half-space of dimension greater than zero. A third is to confuse the intersection property with a union property. Convexity survives intersections and can fail for unions. A fourth, once equalities and nonnegativity are the description, is to accept a solution of \(B x_B = b\) without checking the sign of \(x_B\). That point may leave the polyhedron.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Constructing a basic feasible solution is the algebra behind the vertex test: pick independent columns, solve, and keep the point only when it is nonnegative. A linear objective that is bounded on a nonempty polyhedron of this form attains its optimum at one of those points. Later, a method that minimizes a linear model over a polyhedron can ask only for an extreme point of that model.
